results.title_inferred: Mugwort (Artemisia vulgaris) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine
results.original_text: Norse / Old Norse: Mugwort; also recorded as 'Singrene' in Scandinavian herbal tradition. Old English cognate: 'mucgwyrt' (Nine Herb Charm, Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE). Henrik Harpestraeng, Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE): earliest Danish medical text to record the plant in a Scandinavian clinical context. Icelandic manuscripts: AM 434a (13th–15th century). Note: 'Singrene' may reflect conflation with periwinkle (Vinca minor) in some Scandinavian manuscript traditions; the Nine Herb Charm explicitly names Mugwort as the first and foremost of the nine sacred herbs, invoking it in relation to Woden (Odin): 'Þu eart wyrt wyrta / þu miht wið þreo and wið þritig / þu miht wið attre and wið onflyge / þu miht wið þam laþan / ðe geond lond færð' ('You are the oldest of herbs / you have power against three and against thirty / you have power against poison and against infection / you have power against the loathsome one that travels through the land').
results.translation: In Norse and Scandinavian medicine, Mugwort (Artemisia vulgaris) held a position of supreme ritual and therapeutic authority, named the first of the Nine Sacred Herbs in the Old English Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, c.1000 CE) and explicitly linked to Woden [Odin], who is invoked as its divine originator — suggesting the plant carried deep cosmological significance across the Germanic–Norse continuum. It was employed by Völur [Norse seeresses and shamanic practitioners] and healers alike as a protective and purifying herb, used in fumigation rites to ward off malevolent spirits, 'flying venom' [onflyge — airborne disease or magical contagion], and poisoning. Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) records it in a Danish clinical context for digestive ailments, menstrual regulation, and as a treatment for weariness of travellers, reflecting its dual identity as both a sacred ritual plant and a practical medicinal herb throughout the Norse and Scandinavian world.

The Nine Herb Charm names it first among nine herbs, associating it directly with Woden/Odin.

The Old Norse form of the plant name and its appearance in Harpestraeng and the AM 434a Icelandic manuscripts confirm continuity of the plant's medicinal use across the Scandinavian world. 'Singrene' as a plant name in Scandinavian sources warrants caution: in some manuscript contexts it denotes Vinca minor (periwinkle) rather than Artemisia vulgaris; the identification here follows the Nine Herb Charm and Harpestraeng's primary identification. results.title_inferred: Plantain (Wegbrade) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine — Nine Herb Charm Plant 2
results.original_text: Plantago lanceolata — Norse/Old English: Wegbrade (lit. 'way-broad,' from Old English weg 'way/road' + brad 'broad,' referencing the plant's growth along trackways and its broad-ribbed leaves). Named as the second of nine sacred herbs in the Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE): 'And þu, wegbrade, wyrta modor' ('And you, Wegbrade, mother of plants'). Referenced in Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) under Danish vernacular name. Attested in Icelandic medical manuscripts (AM 434a, 13th–15th century) as a wound herb. No confirmed runic inscription attests the plant by name, but the Nine Herb Charm itself is considered a [galdor] — a spoken magical incantation — invoking Woden (Odin) as the originator of the nine herbs.
results.translation: In the Nine Herb Charm, Wegbrade (ribwort plantain) is addressed as 'mother of plants' [wyrta modor], signalling its pre-eminent status among healing herbs in the Norse-influenced Anglo-Saxon medical tradition; the charm attributes its power ultimately to Woden, who is said to have 'set and sent' the nine herbs against poison and infection. In Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum, the plant appears as a reliable vulnerary [wound herb] and treatment for internal flux, consistent with its use across the broader Scandinavian manuscript tradition. Archaeological evidence from Viking-Age burial contexts — including plant remains associated with female graves interpreted as those of Völur [seeresses/shamanic practitioners] — suggests plantain may have been carried as a medicinal or ritual component alongside other herb assemblages, though direct botanical identification from such sites remains tentative.
results.preparation: In the Nine Herb Charm tradition, Wegbrade was prepared as part of a compound salve: the herb was pounded together with the other eight sacred plants, mixed with soap and old lard (rendered animal fat), apple juice, and the ashes of burnt herbs, then applied externally to wounds or infected skin while the galdor charm was sung aloud — the spoken incantation was inseparable from the physical preparation. Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum recommends the expressed juice of plantain leaves for internal conditions (flux, gastric complaints), and a poultice of bruised fresh leaves for wounds and ulcers. Icelandic manuscripts similarly describe topical application of crushed leaves or a decoction for wound cleansing.
results.condition: Wound healing (cuts, festering sores, ulcers); protection against and treatment of poison [lybb] and venom (snake, insect); internal flux and gastric disorders; infection and putrefaction; ritual/magical protection from malevolent forces [aelf-shot, worm, wen, flying venom] as enumerated in the Nine Herb Charm.

results.title_inferred: Watercress in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine
results.original_text: Stune (Old Norse/Anglo-Saxon: 'stune' or 'wegbrade stune'); Nasturtium officinale. Attested as the third herb in the Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE): 'Stune heo hatte, on stane geweox, stond heo wið attre, stunað heo wærce' ('Stune she is called, on stone she grew, she withstands poison, she attacks pain'). Referenced in Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) under cognate Scandinavian names for aquatic cress. Archaeological trace evidence of Nasturtium officinale seeds and plant material recovered from Viking-Age waterlogged contexts in Scandinavia and the Danelaw.
results.translation: In the Nine Herb Charm, Stune (Watercress) is invoked as the third sacred herb in a nine-part medicinal incantation attributed to Woden [Odin], who is described as having created these nine herbs to combat the nine causes of disease spread by the 'worm' [serpent or malevolent force]; the charm explicitly connects Stune's power to its stony, waterside growing habit — its rootedness in harsh terrain signifying its potency against poison and bodily pain. Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum and related Scandinavian herbal traditions record watercress as a cooling, purifying plant used to draw out venomous afflictions, treat skin eruptions, and support the liver and blood — consistent with its biochemical properties as a source of volatile mustard oils and vitamin C. Völva [Norse seeress] and seiðr [magic/shamanic healing] practices, as inferred from Eddic and saga sources, incorporated such water-dwelling plants in ritual preparations believed to dissolve corrupted matter within the body, aligning Stune with the Norse concept of 'lyfjaberg' [herb-mountain or healing herb] as described in the Eddic poem Sigrdrífumál.

preparation.dosage: No precise Viking-Age dosage survives for Stune specifically. Harpestraeng's broader tradition suggests fresh plant juice or decoction. The Nine Herb Charm prescribes the herbs to be ground together ('gegnid') into a powder or salve, combined with soap and apple juice, mixed with water and ash, and applied externally as a poultice to wounds or taken as a drink. Watercress was likely also consumed raw or boiled as a pot-herb [green vegetable medicine], consistent with its widespread availability in Norse waterways.
preparation.method: Grinding of dried or fresh herb; combination with other Eight Charm herbs (Mugwort, Cockspur Grass, Lamb's Cress, Plantain, Mayweed, Nettle, Crab Apple, Thyme/Chervil) into a compound salve or medicinal drink; ritual verbal incantation recited during preparation as integral to efficacy.

results.title_inferred: Cockspur Grass (Chickweed) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine
results.original_text: Norse/Old Norse: Stithe (also rendered Stiðe or Styðe). The Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE) names this herb as the fourth of nine sacred plants, listing it alongside Mugwort, Waybread, and Nettle in a verse formula invoking Woden's act of creation. Old Norse stiðr carries connotations of 'stiff' or 'strong,' possibly referencing the plant's vigorous spreading habit or its stiffening/hardening medicinal action. No confirmed runic inscription names this plant directly, though the Nine Herb Charm itself functions as a verbal [galdr]-charm, a sung or spoken incantation of the type associated with Norse seiðr and völva practice.
results.translation: In the Nine Herb Charm, Stiðe (identified by most scholars with Stellaria media, common chickweed, though the identification remains contested) is presented as one of nine plants created or empowered by Woden [Óðinn], giving it explicit divine sanction within the Germanic healing tradition. The charm instructs that these nine herbs, including Stiðe, possess power against nine causes of disease — venom, flying venom, and malignant spirits among them — and the plant was employed in compound wound-salves and poultice preparations intended to draw out poison and infection. In Scandinavian folk practice aligned with völva healing traditions, cooling, moisture-retaining plants such as chickweed were applied to inflamed or 'hot' wounds, connecting the herb's known emollient properties to a broader humoral and magical framework in which Woden's nine herbs counteracted the nine sources of supernatural illness.

Appears as the fifth plant in the Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE): referenced as a healing herb of Woden alongside mugwort, plantain, watercress, and others. No confirmed runic inscription names chamomile directly, though aromatic botanical remains consistent with Matricaria chamomilla have been recovered from Viking-age burial and settlement contexts in Scandinavia.

Henrik Harpestraeng records chamomile in the Liber Herbarum under its Latinised name as a remedy for digestive ailments, inflammation, and female complaints, situating it firmly within the learned Galenic-Norse medical tradition of 13th-century Denmark. Völva [seeress] and healer figures in Old Norse society likely employed strongly aromatic herbs such as chamomile in ritual fumigation and charm-work, consistent with its documented dual role as both medicinal and apotropaic plant across the Germanic world.

results.title_inferred: Crab Apple (Wergulu) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine
results.original_text: Norse/Old Norse: Wergulu (also attested as 'wergul' or 'wiergulu' in Old English cognate forms of the Nine Herb Charm, Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE). The name is of disputed etymology; most scholars derive it from Proto-Germanic *wer- (man, protection) or connect it to Old Norse 'vörðr' (guardian, warden), suggesting a protective or apotropaic function. No direct runic inscriptions name the crab apple, but the Nine Herb Charm identifies Wergulu as the sixth of nine sacred herbs, invoking Woden (Óðinn) as the deity who established its power: 'A snake came crawling, it bit a man. Then Woden took nine glory-twigs, smote the adder so that it flew into nine parts.' The crab apple's inclusion among the nine suggests its role in the broader Norse and Germanic cosmological framework, wherein sacred plants mediated between the human and divine realms.
results.translation: In the Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585), Wergulu — the crab apple (Malus sylvestris) — is listed as the sixth of nine herbs empowered by Woden (Óðinn) to combat poison, infection, and malevolent forces, placing it firmly within a magico-medical tradition that blurs the boundary between herbalism and ritual invocation. Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE), the oldest extant Danish medical text, records apple-derived preparations for digestive complaints, fevers, and wound treatment, likely drawing on a continuous Scandinavian folk tradition that predates the Christian manuscript context. Archaeological evidence from Viking burial sites — including carbonised crab apple remains at Hedeby and Birka — suggests the fruit held both dietary and probable ritual significance, consistent with the Völva [seeress/shamanic practitioner] tradition of carrying herb-filled pouches or 'staff-bags' containing magically potent plants for healing and protective seiðr [Norse shamanic magic] workings.
